'''''Lysimachia foemina''''' is [[common name|commonly]] known as '''blue pimpernel'''<ref>Clive Stace, ''New Flora of the British Isles'' 4th edition 2019, p 552</ref> or '''poor man's weatherglass''', and was formerly called '''''Anagallis foemina'''''. It is a low-growing [[Annual plant|annual]] [[herbaceous]] plant in the genus ''[[Lysimachia]]'' of the family [[Primulaceae]]. In a comparison of [[DNA sequence]]s, ''L. foemina'' was shown to be most closely [[Phylogenetics|related]] to ''L. monelli''.<ref name="manns2007">{{cite journal | last = Manns | first = Ulrika |author2=Anderberg, AA | title = Relationships of ''Anagallis foemina'' and ''Anagallis arvensis'' (Myrsinaceae): New insights inferred from DNA sequence data | journal = Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution | volume = 45 | issue = 3 | pages = 971–980 | date = Dec 2007 | doi = 10.1016/j.ympev.2007.07.022 | pmid=17869544}}</ref> It had been thought by many to be closest to ''[[Lysimachia arvensis|L. arvensis]]'', and some authors had even included ''L. foemina'' as a [[subspecies]] of ''L. arvensis'', as  '''''Anagallis arvensis'' subsp. ''foemina'''''.<ref>Clapham, Tutin, & Warburg: ''Flora of the British Isles'', 2nd edition, page 435</ref> These three species (''L arvensis'', ''L foemina'' and ''L monelli'') were among several transferred from ''[[Anagallis]]'' to ''[[Lysimachia]]'' in a 2009 paper.<ref>{{cite journal|title= New combinations and names in ''Lysimachia'' (Myrsinaceae) for species of ''Anagallis'', ''Pelletiera'' and ''Trientalis''|author1=Manns, Ulrika |author2=Anderberg, Arne A. |date=July 2009|journal=Willdenowia|pages=49–54|volume=39|issue=1|jstor=20699148|doi=10.3372/wi.39.39103|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Etymology==
The previous genus name ''Anagallis'' derives from the Greek words ''{{lang|el|ana}}'' meaning "again" and ''{{lang|el|agallein}}'' meaning "to delight in", possibly referring to the fact that these plants produce flowers twice in a year and the flowers open whenever the sun strikes them.<ref name=malta>{{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20070701152638/http://www.maltawildplants.com/PRIM/Anagallis_foemina.html|title=Malta Wild Plants}}</ref> The [[specific name (botany)|species epithet]] ''{{lang|la|foemina}}'' means "female" and refers to the small size of the plant and the gentleness of its appearance. The common name refers to the fact that the flowers close at the approaching of the bad weather.<ref name=Trek>[http://www.treknature.com/gallery/photo149739.htm Trek Nature]</ref>

==Description==
''Lysimachia foemina'' has weak, square and sprawling stems growing to about {{convert|5|-|18|cm}} long,<ref name=Pignatti>Pignatti S. - Flora d'Italia – Edagricole – 1982. Vol. II, pag. 291</ref> which bear bright green sessile leaves in opposite pairs. The leaves are usually lance-shaped about {{convert|7|-|11|mm|abbr=on}} wide and {{convert|12|-|16|mm|abbr=on}} long, although some leaves, especially the lowest, may be ovate.

The small flowers are about {{convert|8|mm|abbr=on}} in diameter, have a short stalk, are produced in the leaf axils and are usually blue. They have five lanceolate [[sepal]]s and five petals. The [[filament (botany)|filament]]s are about {{convert|3|mm|abbr=on}} long, with showy yellow [[anther]]s. The flowering period extends from April to October.<ref name=Pignatti/> The [[Hermaphrodite|hermaphroditic]] flowers are pollinated by insects ([[entomogamy]]). The fruit is a spherical capsule up to {{convert|4|mm|abbr=on}} in diameter containing about 15 seeds.<ref name=Pignatti/>

This species is very similar to the related ''[[Lysimachia arvensis]]'', and has been regarded as a subspecies of ''L arvensis''. In 2007, a molecular phylogenetic study showed that ''Lysimachia foemina'' is more closely related to ''[[Lysimachia monelli]]'' than to ''[[Lysimachia arvensis]]'', and should be treated as a separate species.<ref name="manns2007"/>

===Confusable Species===
''Lysimachia foemina'' is widely confused with [[Lysimachia loeflingii]] (formerly ''Lysimachia arvensis var. azurea/caerulea''). They can be distinguished by the large fruiting capsule's conspicuous veins (loeflingii 5-6 veined, foemina many more), petal shape/glanding (foemina narrow, separated petals with sparse (3)4-celled glands at tip (final cell ellipsoid), loeflingii usually broad touching petals with many 3-celled glands (final cell globose) (see photo in Stace<ref name="Stace"/>)), flower stalk (foemina most stalks up to length of under-flower leaves, loeflingii often much longer), leaf shape/colour (foemina upper leaves rather narrow and usually dark, loeflingii broader and usually lighter).<ref name="Stace">New Flora of the British Isles, ed. 4 and also 3, C. Stace</ref><ref name="FoT">{{cite book |title=Flora of Turkey and the East Aegean Islands, vol. 6 |author=Davis}}</ref><ref name="FBI3">{{cite book |title=Flora of the British Isles, ed. 3 |author=Tutin}}</ref>

==Distribution==
This cosmopolitan plant is native to central and southern [[Europe]] and has been introduced in [[Africa]], northern and eastern [[Asia]], North and South [[Americas|America]] and western [[Australia]].<ref name=Pignatti/>

==Habitat==
It grows in scrub, uncultivated soils and grasslands. It prefers dry, nutrient- and lime-rich soils, at an altitude of {{convert|0|-|1200|m}} above sea level.<ref name=Pignatti/>
